content:
Hold on until the last moment

"To be honest, I held on until the last moment." The two sisters grew up in Wang Fuk Court with their parents. After their father passed away and the elder sister got married, Ms Yuen lived with her mother until the fire. Her mother died in the blaze. During the period of going upstairs, she once wore a sweater with the handwritten words "rebuild on the original site" to express her demand. But the authorities rejected it, and the owners' committee refused to discuss it. It was not until one week before the 31 August acquisition deadline that she submitted a "letter accepting the acquisition proposal".

Ms Yuen believes the residents of Wang Fuk Court have already been "crushed like a crab under a boulder". She said the two explainers she had contacted in the past could not answer her questions, and their only clear goal was to press residents on whether they had sold their flats.

Post-disaster life is "living in a borrowed place"

Since the fire, Ms Yuen has stayed at Sin Lau in Tai Po and later moved to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a "temporary residence fee" every month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet that once filled the flat, as well as the neighbours and security guards, constantly remind her of her status. She describes her life after the incident as "living in a borrowed place".

Rethinking what "home" means

Every day after work, she returns to this empty flat at eight or nine o'clock, and on holidays she chooses to leave and go to her sister's home. "Actually, after the incident, I started thinking here about what 'home' means, what 'a home' means. A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when this home at Wang Fuk Court can also be burned down…"

"The word 'home' is quite heavy for me now"

When the reporter asked Ms Yuen about her idea of home, she said the old phone that held the photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories remain only in her mind. She sighed deeply and said, "(Home) is not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, a full set of home appliances for me to have what is called a proper home. It makes me rethink what the elements inside a proper home really are, so I cannot answer this question for now, because the word 'home' is quite heavy for me now."

Dissatisfied with the officials' "let go" remarks

The responses of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire, such as the "let go" remarks by Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing and the talk of market value by Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun, have only deepened her frustration and anger. "The more you stay silent, the less I understand." "When they can actually say such cold and unfeeling words, what do they really think about the meaning of home?"

A sense of being "sold cheap"

Recalling the instant she signed the letter accepting the acquisition, Ms Yuen said the strongest feelings were unwillingness and a sense of being "sold cheap", because a home is not only its material value but also its emotional and memory ties. "The flat was something my father and mother worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken away from us for nothing, compared with being 'sold cheap' now, I am even more unwilling."

After signing the letter, Ms Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has delayed the submission of its report until October. Ms Yuen said pursuing accountability is one part of it, "but how I personally move on, I cannot answer. Because from the incident until now, my life feels like a total loss. First, the home was destroyed, and what that destruction means is that it is as if the history of my growing up has been wiped away. A family member also died in the fire, and it was a sudden death… There is a huge hole in my heart. Can this hole truly be filled? Or will there be a day when it can heal? I do not know how to answer."
